name: Neuwieder Green
lede: Neuwieder Green is a light, yellowish green that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates to around 1850, likely after the German town of Neuwied, known historically for its dye and chemical works.

sections.title: A town's name, a tentative date
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul place this value at plate 17, position B 8, first recorded around 1850, the "c." in their own record signaling that the date is approximate rather than exact [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 classifies it as a light yellowish green, about 3.4 units from that block's reference chip [2]. Our library's note gives no direct statement that the name refers to Neuwied on the Rhine, so the connection, however likely for a nineteenth-century German dye name, remains unconfirmed here [1].

Its nearest library neighbor is [[celadon|Celadon]], and it sits close to [[cobalt-green|Cobalt Green]], [[baby-green|Baby Green]] and [[seafoam-green|Seafoam Green]] on the same light, yellow-green stretch of the chart [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Neuwieder Green covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 6 works, as photographed [3]. Two of those six are by Van Gogh, *Roulin's Baby* and a still life of oranges and lemons, both from 1888 and 1889 [3]. It functions mostly as a highlight color and is most over-represented in paintings from Austria [3]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished canvases read as screen colors, not pigment tests [3].
